title: Tell me about a time you had to make a decision with incomplete information: how did you proceed?
shortTitle: Making a Decision With Incomplete Information: how did you proceed?
keyPoints: Gather what you can quickly, then decide rather than freezing.
Favor the safest reversible option when stakes are high and information is incomplete.
Assess the worst-case cost of each option before choosing.
Communicate your assumptions explicitly so the team can challenge them.
Set a checkpoint to revisit and adjust as new data arrives.
One-way-door decisions deserve more deliberation; two-way-door decisions deserve less.
Calibrated action under uncertainty is the mark of a senior engineer.

s1_definition.oneliner: When information is incomplete, gather what you can quickly, favor the reversible safe option, decide, and adjust as new facts arrive.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Act, do not freeze** – Decide with the best available information rather than waiting for perfection.
- **Reversibility bias** – Under uncertainty, favor the option that is easiest to undo.
- **Worst-case assessment** – For each option, ask: what is the worst that happens if I am wrong?
- **Explicit assumptions** – State what you are assuming so others can challenge it.
- **Checkpoint** – Set a time to revisit and adjust as new data arrives.
- **One-way vs two-way** – Invest more deliberation in irreversible decisions.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine during a production incident at National Bank of India, you must decide whether to pause all transfers while investigating a suspected double-charge on Priya's account, but you do not yet know how widespread it is. You weigh the cost of acting versus waiting, favor the reversible safe option, and refine as you learn more.

sections.s6_takeaway:
At National Bank of India, our monitoring showed a spike in failed transfers with signs of possible double-processing on accounts like Priya's. I did not yet know how widespread it was or the root cause. I had to decide quickly whether to keep running, throttle, or pause transfers.

I assessed each option by worst-case cost and reversibility. Keeping the system running had the highest worst-case cost : a widespread double-charge is hard to undo. Pausing had the lowest worst-case cost and was fully reversible. So I chose to pause, communicated my assumptions explicitly, and set a checkpoint to revisit in fifteen minutes.

Within that time we confirmed the issue was limited, fixed the root cause, and resumed transfers, having prevented any large-scale double-charge. The brief pause was a small availability cost that prevented a much larger financial one.

What I learned is that decisions with incomplete information are not about guessing. They are about gathering what you can quickly, weighing worst-case cost and reversibility, choosing the safest reversible path, and adjusting fast as facts arrive.

Remember one sentence: Under uncertainty, favor the safest reversible option, state your assumptions explicitly, and set a checkpoint to adjust as new data arrives.
